title: What is known about 1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB.
intro: Nobody knows whether this six-state, two-symbol Turing machine halts when started on a blank tape: it is one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: Open, Collatz-like, reduced in Lean to an explicit map. It is a Lean theorem (kernel-checked) that the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of one configuration under an explicit map G on two lists of block lengths halts. The tape is a list of blocks of 1s with the head between two of them; a long block next to an empty one is dismantled two 1s at a time, half going to each neighbour, down to 2 or 3 ones by its parity. The machine halts exactly when the blocks left of the head are used up, which needs every one of them to be 111 at the same moment; for a lone block that means 3·(2m − 1) ones. The orbit has been followed for 109 applications of the accelerated map (1.5·1024 steps of the machine) without a halt.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (C0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 6,721 cells have been visited and 6,706 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: power/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.27). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.357).

claims.title: Shift rules of the sweeps
claims.text: The head crosses blocks of 1s: L (1)^n A>1 R to the left and L E> (1)^n R to the right, one step a cell, for every n and all tapes L, R.

claims.title: The map G on two lists of block lengths
claims.text: At the moments the head is in state B on a 0 with a block of 1s directly on its left, the tape is … 0 1g2 0 1g1 B> 0 1b0 000 1b1 000 …: blocks separated by one 0 on the left and by 000 on the right. Call it v gs bs with the two lists of block lengths. G is an explicit computable map from one such moment to the next, with five cases by the length k of the block next to the head (k = 1, 2, 3, k ≥ 4, and no block: halt). The theorem G_sem says, for every such configuration x and with nothing assumed: if G x is a configuration y, the machine goes from x to y in at least one step; if G x is undefined, the machine halts from x. The proofs compose the two proved block crossings with single steps.

claims.title: Halts iff the orbit of G halts
claims.text: The machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of v [1] [] (the tape 1 B> 0 after the first step) under G reaches a configuration where G is undefined. Those are exactly the configurations with no block (or an empty block) left of the head (G_none_iff).

claims.title: The transfer loop, and the fast map GA
claims.text: When the block next to the head has K ≥ 4 ones and the first block on the right is empty, two applications of G take two 1s from the block and give one to the next block on each side, and the situation repeats: the block is dismantled down to 2 (K even) or 3 (K odd) ones, half of it going left and half right (loop, proved by induction for every K). GA is G with this loop done in one application; halts_iff_fast is the same equivalence for GA: the machine halts from blank tape iff the orbit of v [1] [] under GA halts.

claims.title: A lone block of 3·(2<sup>m</sup> − 1) ones halts
claims.text: If the left list is a single block of 3·(2<sup>m+1</sup> − 1) ones (3, 9, 21, 45, 93, …) and the first block on the right is empty, the orbit under GA halts 2m + 2 applications later: the loop turns a lone block of 2j + 5 ones into a lone block of j + 1, and a lone block of 3 is erased, which leaves nothing left of the head.

claims.title: No halt in the first 20,000 applications of GA
No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> applications of GA
claims.text: The same by compiled evaluation. By the step counts of c/vsa.c (trusted) this is 1.9·1018 steps of the machine.

claims.title: No halt in the first 1.5·10<sup>24</sup> steps
claims.text: The C program c/vsa.c follows GA with exact step counts (128-bit integers): no halt in the first 109 applications of GA, which stand for 1016 applications of G and 1,508,121,318,047,435,715,005,702 steps of the machine; the tape then holds 988,764,137 ones. The maps and their step counts are checked against a direct simulation cell by cell for the first 20,000 configurations (py/vmap.py check).

claims.title: A halt is neither excluded nor likely soon
claims.text: The left list is down to a single block about once in 180 applications of GA, and that block is then of the size of the tape; the machine halts there only if the block has exactly 3·(2<sup>m</sup> − 1) ones (or in one of a few similar exact coincidences of small blocks). If these blocks behaved like random numbers this would give an expected number of halts of the order of 0.01 each time the tape doubles, for ever. In the first 10<sup>8</sup> applications of GA a lone block had fewer than 16 ones only 16 times, and never 3 or 9 ones.

claims.title: Does it halt from blank tape?
claims.text: Not known. By halts_iff the question is exactly whether the orbit of G ever uses up the list of blocks left of the head, which needs all of them to be 111 at once: a Collatz-like question about one explicit orbit of block lists.

check: python3 holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB/py/rules.py | diff - holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB/lean/Rules.lean   # the rules file is current
cd holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB && python3 py/vmap.py check 20000   # the maps G and GA against the machine
cd holdouts/1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1LA0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB && gcc -O2 -o vsa c/vsa.c && ./vsa 1e9 0   # the orbit of GA with step counts (6 s; 1e12 takes about 100 minutes)

explainer.lede: Nobody knows. The tape is a list of blocks of 1s, and the head keeps cutting the block next to it in half, one half for each neighbour. Lean proves that the machine halts exactly when one explicit orbit of block lists runs out of blocks on the left, which takes an exact coincidence such as a lone block of 3·(2^m − 1) ones: a question about the binary digits of a number, like Collatz.

facts.text: Proved in Lean: halting from blank tape is exactly the orbit question for the map G on two block lists.
No halt: 10<sup>9</sup> applications of the accelerated map, followed with exact step counts by a C program.
No halt, proved in Lean (1.9·10<sup>18</sup> steps); the first 20,000 by the kernel alone.
The length of a lone left block that would halt the machine.

sections.heading: Two lists of blocks, the head between them
html: Look at the machine at the moments its head is in state B on a 0 with a block of 1s directly on its left. The tape is then always a list of blocks of 1s: separated by a single 0 on the left of the head and by 000 on the right.
What happens next depends only on k, the length of the block next to the head (g is the block after it, b the first block on the right; either is 0 when absent):

• k ≥ 4: the block loses two 1s, the block g gains one, and the block b (three longer) moves to the left of the head: … 1^(g+1) 0 1^(k−2) 0 1^(b+3) B> 0 ….
  • k = 3: the block is erased; one 1 goes to the first block on the right, and an empty block appears in front of it: … 1^g B> 0 000 1^(b+1) 000 ….
  • k = 2: … 0 1^(g+2) 0 1^(b+2) B> 0 … (and the block left of g gains one).
  • k = 1: the blocks g, 1 and b merge into one.
  • no block left of the head: B writes a 1, C reads a 0, and the machine halts.

Put k ≥ 4 and k = 3 together: when the first block on the right is empty (b = 0), the block that moves left has exactly three 1s and is erased at once. The net effect is that the block k has lost two 1s and each neighbour has gained one, and the same happens again. A long block is dismantled this way, half of it going left and half right, down to 2 ones if it was even and 3 if it was odd:

sections.heading: The map G, proved
html: Write v gs bs for the configuration with the list gs of blocks left of the head (nearest first) and the list bs of blocks right of it, and let inc j add j to the first entry of a list. The whole machine is this table:

fromto
v [] bshalt
v (1 :: g :: gs) (b :: bs) → v ((g + b + 3) :: inc 2 gs) bs
v (2 :: g :: gs) (b :: bs)v ((b + 2) :: (g + 2) :: inc 1 gs) bs
v (3 :: gs) bsv gs (0 :: inc 1 bs)
v (k :: gs) (b :: bs), k ≥ 4v ((b + 3) :: (k − 2) :: inc 1 gs) bs

Every row is a Lean theorem for all values (G_sem in lean/Map.lean): the machine really goes from the left configuration to the right one, in at least one step. After its first step from blank tape the machine is at v [1] [], so the machine halts from blank tape if and only if the orbit of v [1] [] under G reaches the first row (halts_iff). Nothing is assumed in that statement. The only difference from the sibling machine 1RB1LA_1LC0RE_---0LD_1RE0LF_1RA1RE_1LA0LB is the row for k = 1.

The dismantling of a long block is proved once and for all (loop), which gives a second map GA that does it in one application, with the same theorem (halts_iff_fast). GA is cheap to iterate: a C program with exact step counts (c/vsa.c) has followed it for 109 applications, which is 1.5·1024 steps of the machine, without a halt. Lean itself checks the first 107 applications (1.9·1018 steps).

sections.heading: Running out of blocks on the left
html: Blocks left of the head are never empty (every row puts blocks of at least 2 there), so the machine halts in one way only: the list on the left is used up. Only the row k = 3 shortens it without putting something back, so at that moment every block left of the head must be 111.

The typical way to get there: the left list is down to a single long block of x ones, with an empty block on the right. The dismantling turns x = 2j + 5 into a lone block of j + 1 (the half that went left), so x + 3 is halved; this repeats as long as the numbers stay odd. If x = 3·(2m − 1) (3, 9, 21, 45, 93, …) the chain ends on a lone 111, which is erased, and the machine halts (Lean: bottom_halts). For any other x an even number turns up and the head goes back to the right.

The left list is down to a single block about once in 180 applications of GA, with a block of the size of the tape. If these blocks behaved like random numbers, hitting 3·(2m − 1) exactly would add up to an expected number of halts of the order of 0.01 each time the tape doubles, for ever: a halt is not excluded by any residue argument we know, and it is not likely soon. This estimate is a heuristic.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like a power of the step count other than 1/2 (fitted exponent 0.27). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.357).
After 109 steps the tape spans 6,721 cells (145 left of the start, 5,176 right), with a density of 1s of 0.998.

summary: Blocks of 1s on both sides of the head; a long block next to an empty one is dismantled, half to each neighbour, ending in 2 or 3 ones by parity. Lean proves that the machine halts iff the orbit of an explicit map on the two block lists uses up the left list (a lone block of 3(2^m - 1) ones, or a run of blocks 111 to the left end); no halt in 1.5·10^24 steps.
family: unary blocks split in halves, Collatz-like
